existing.description_long: A 2017 Fair Labor Association audit of a Chinese factory producing Ivanka Trump-branded clothing for licensing partner G-III Apparel found the facility violated two dozen standards set by the U.N. International Labor Organization: workers earned roughly $62 per week — at or below China's minimum wage — endured excessive hours, lacked legally mandated pension and medical benefits, and received only five days of paid leave per year. Average urban Chinese manufacturing wages were nearly double what Ivanka's supply chain paid. Separately, in 2016, a blog post written by one of Ivanka's own interns detailed how to survive New York City on zero salary, revealing that the brand relied on unpaid interns for copywriting, marketing, licensing, and graphic design. The exposure drew immediate criticism from labor lawyers who argued the arrangement likely violated the Fair Labor Standards Act. Net sales for the Ivanka Trump collection grew by $17.9 million in 2016 — the year her father was elected — despite boycott campaigns.
